A: No — it's the legal minimum. Non-unionized employees dismissed without cause are usually entitled to common-law 'reasonable notice', which can be several months and far exceeds the ESA/Code minimums. Get legal advice before signing a release.
Q: Does this apply if I quit or was fired for cause?
A: Statutory termination and severance generally don't apply if you resign or are dismissed for wilful misconduct/just cause. They apply to without-cause terminations and layoffs.

### Canada Vacation Pay Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/canada/vacation-pay-calculator/
Vacation pay is a percentage of your gross wages — 4% or 6% in Ontario, and 4%/6%/8% federally by length of service. Estimate what you've earned or are owed on leaving.
#### How it is calculated
Rule | Detail
Ontario — under 5 years | 4% of gross wages (2 weeks vacation)
Ontario — 5+ years | 6% of gross wages (3 weeks vacation)
Federal — 1 to 5 years | 4% of gross wages (2 weeks)
Federal — 5 to 10 years | 6% of gross wages (3 weeks)
Federal — 10+ years | 8% of gross wages (4 weeks)
On leaving | All accrued unpaid vacation pay must be paid out
Vacation pay is calculated on gross wages (excluding vacation pay itself). Federally, the 8% tier at 10 years is the key difference from Ontario, which tops out at 6%. Source: ontario.ca / canada.ca .
#### Questions
Q: How is vacation pay calculated in Ontario?
A: It's 4% of your gross wages if you've been employed under 5 years (equivalent to 2 weeks' vacation), and 6% once you reach 5 years (3 weeks). On leaving, any vacation pay you've accrued but not taken must be paid out.
Q: What is the federal vacation pay rate?
A: Under the Canada Labour Code it's 4% after 1 year (2 weeks), 6% after 5 consecutive years (3 weeks), and 8% after 10 consecutive years (4 weeks). The 8% tier is the main difference from Ontario, which caps at 6%.
Q: Do I get vacation pay when I quit or am fired?
A: Yes. Vacation pay accrues on your wages regardless of how the job ends, so any accrued but unpaid vacation pay must be included in your final pay.
Q: Is vacation pay calculated on gross or net wages?
A: On gross wages — your earnings before deductions — and generally excluding vacation pay already paid. Overtime and most wages count toward the base it's calculated on.
Q: Does vacation pay come on top of severance?
A: Yes. Vacation pay is a separate entitlement from termination and severance pay, and all accrued vacation pay is owed in your final settlement.

## Australia

### Australia Annual Leave Payout Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/australia/annual-leave-calculator/
Turn your accrued unused annual leave into a payout figure for when you leave. The NES gives 4 weeks a year, paid out on termination at your base rate — plus 17.5% loading where it applies.
#### How it is calculated
Rule | Detail
NES entitlement | 4 weeks paid annual leave per year (5 for some shift workers)
Accrual | Progressive — ≈2.923 hours per 38 ordinary hours worked
On termination | All accrued unused annual leave must be paid out
Pay basis | Base rate for ordinary hours
Leave loading | 17.5% (if it applied) is paid out even if the award says otherwise
Annual leave loading is not part of the NES — it comes from an award or agreement — but where it applied during employment, Fair Work says it is paid out on termination. Source: Fair Work Ombudsman — Final pay & annual leave .
#### Questions
Q: Do I get paid for unused annual leave when I leave in Australia?
A: Yes. Under the National Employment Standards, all accrued but unused annual leave must be paid out when your employment ends, at the same amount you'd have received had you taken it — your base rate for ordinary hours.
Q: How much annual leave do you accrue in Australia?
A: The NES gives 4 weeks of paid annual leave per year (5 weeks for certain shift workers). It accrues progressively — roughly 2.923 hours for every 38 ordinary hours worked — and carries over year to year.
Q: Is annual leave loading paid out on termination?
A: If a 17.5% annual leave loading applied to you during employment (through an award or enterprise agreement), Fair Work states it must be paid out on your accrued leave when you leave — even if the award says loading isn't payable on termination.
Q: What rate is annual leave paid out at?
A: At your base rate of pay for ordinary hours (capped at 38 hours a week under the NES). This excludes overtime and penalty rates, but includes leave loading where it applied.
Q: How do I find my accrued leave balance?
A: Australian payslips show your accrued annual leave, usually in hours. Enter that figure and your base hourly rate to estimate the payout; the tool also shows the rough equivalent in weeks.

### Long Service Leave Calculator (NSW & VIC)
URL: https://calcnate.com/australia/long-service-leave-calculator/
Estimate your long service leave for NSW or Victoria. LSL is STATE-based — every state and territory has its own Act, thresholds and formula. This tool covers NSW and Victoria.
#### How it is calculated
Rule | Detail
NSW — accrual | 2 months (8.67 weeks) after 10 years; +1 month per further 5 years
NSW — pro-rata | Payable at 5–<10 years only if employer ends it (not misconduct), or you resign for illness/pressing necessity, or death
Victoria — accrual | 1/60th of total continuous service (≈8.67 weeks after 10 years)
Victoria — pro-rata | Payable on termination after 7 years, for any reason
Pay basis | Ordinary rate of pay
Other states | QLD, SA, WA, TAS, ACT, NT each differ — not covered here
Long service leave is state-based: thresholds and formulas differ in every jurisdiction. This tool covers NSW and Victoria only — check your own state's Act for others. Source: NSW LSL Act 1955 / Vic LSL Act 2018 .
#### Questions
Q: How much long service leave do you get in NSW?
A: In NSW you're entitled to 2 months (8.67 weeks) of paid long service leave after 10 years of continuous service, plus 1 additional month for every further 5 years. Between 5 and 10 years, a pro-rata amount is only payable if the employer ends your employment (other than for serious misconduct), you resign due to illness/incapacity or pressing necessity, or on death.
Q: How is long service leave calculated in Victoria?
A: Victoria uses a 1/60th rule: you accrue 1/60th of your total period of continuous employment as long service leave (about 8.67 weeks after 10 years). You can take leave after 7 years, and if your job ends after 7 years the pro-rata balance is paid out — regardless of who ended it.
Q: Is long service leave the same in every state?
A: No. Long service leave is set by each state and territory's own Act, and the thresholds and formulas differ. This calculator covers NSW and Victoria; Queensland, SA, WA, Tasmania, the ACT and NT each have separate rules you should check.
Q: Do I get long service leave paid out if I resign?
A: It depends on your state and service. In Victoria, yes, once you have 7+ years. In NSW, only at 10+ years for an ordinary resignation; between 5 and 10 years an ordinary resignation doesn't qualify (illness/pressing-necessity resignations do).
Q: What pay rate is long service leave paid at?
A: Long service leave is paid at your ordinary rate of pay. This calculator applies your weekly ordinary pay to the accrued weeks.

### Australia Redundancy Pay Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/australia/redundancy-pay-calculator/
Your National Employment Standards (NES) redundancy pay — a set number of weeks by length of continuous service, paid at your base rate. Fair Work Act 2009.
#### How it is calculated
Rule | Detail
1 – <2 years | 4 weeks
2 – <3 years | 6 weeks
3 – <4 years | 7 weeks
4 – <5 years | 8 weeks
5 – <6 years | 10 weeks
6 – <7 years | 11 weeks
7 – <8 years | 13 weeks
8 – <9 years | 14 weeks
9 – <10 years | 16 weeks
10 years or more | 12 weeks (long service leave applies)
Paid at the base rate of pay for ordinary hours (excludes overtime, penalty rates, bonuses and most allowances). Under 1 year = nil. Small-business employers ( Fair Work Ombudsman — Redundancy pay .
#### Questions
Q: How is redundancy pay calculated in Australia?
A: Under the National Employment Standards, redundancy pay is a set number of weeks based on your length of continuous service: 4 weeks at 1 year, rising to a peak of 16 weeks at 9–10 years, then dropping to 12 weeks at 10+ years. It's paid at your base rate of pay for ordinary hours.
Q: Why does redundancy pay drop after 10 years?
A: It's a deliberate feature of the NES scale. Pay peaks at 16 weeks for 9 to under 10 years, then falls to 12 weeks at 10+ years, because employees with 10 years become entitled to long service leave, which offsets the reduction.
Q: Is redundancy pay based on base or gross pay?
A: Base rate of pay for ordinary hours — it excludes overtime, penalty rates, bonuses, commissions and most allowances and loadings. An applicable award or enterprise agreement can treat some allowances differently.
Q: Do small businesses have to pay redundancy pay?
A: Generally no. Employers with fewer than 15 employees are exempt from NES redundancy pay, though a modern award or enterprise agreement may still impose an obligation.
Q: Do I get redundancy pay with under 1 year of service?
A: No NES redundancy pay applies with under 12 months of continuous service, but you may still be owed notice of termination and payout of accrued annual leave.

## Global tools

### Compound Interest Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/compound-interest-calculator/
Project savings growth with regular contributions — and see what the balance is actually worth after inflation.
#### How compound interest is calculated
Compounding | Effective rate | Balance after 1 year
Yearly | 7.000% | 10,700
Half-yearly | 7.123% | 10,712
Quarterly | 7.186% | 10,719
Monthly | 7.229% | 10,723
Daily | 7.250% | 10,725
Continuous | 7.251% | 10,725
Compound interest pays interest on your interest. The balance after t years on a lump sum is: A = P × (1 + r/n) n·t P = starting amount · r = annual rate as a decimal · n = compounding periods per year · t = years. Regular contributions are handled separately, because each one compounds for a different length of time. This calculator converts your nominal rate into an effective annual rate , then into an equivalent monthly rate, and steps through the balance month by month — which is exactly how a savings account or index fund actually behaves. Why compounding frequency matters The same 7% behaves differently depending on how often it is applied. On a 10,000 lump sum over one year: The gap between yearly and daily is small over one year but compounds into a real difference over decades. Why the inflation field matters A balance of 500,000 in thirty years is not 500,000 of today's spending power. Entering an inflation rate divides the final balance by (1 + inflation) years to show the real value — the number that actually tells you what the money will buy.
#### Questions
Q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
A: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount, so 1,000 at 10% earns 100 every year forever. Compound interest is paid on the balance including past interest, so year two earns 110, year three earns 121, and so on. Over long periods the difference is enormous.
Q: Should I use monthly or annual compounding?
A: Use whatever your account actually does. Most savings accounts and loans compound monthly or daily; bonds often pay half-yearly. If you do not know, monthly is the closest approximation for most retail products.
Q: Are contributions added at the start or end of the month?
A: At the end of each month, which is the conservative assumption and matches how most salary-funded savings work. Contributing at the start of the month would produce a slightly higher balance.
Q: What return rate should I assume?
A: That is your judgement, not a fact this tool can supply. For context, long-run global equity returns have historically averaged roughly 7% a year before inflation, but any individual decade can be far higher or lower — including negative.
Q: Does this account for tax?
A: No. Investment and interest income are taxed very differently across countries, so the projection is pre-tax. Reduce your assumed rate if interest is taxed annually where you live.

### Loan & EMI Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/loan-emi-calculator/
Your monthly instalment, the true interest cost, and what overpaying actually saves you.
#### How the EMI is calculated
Every mainstream lender uses the same reducing-balance formula: EMI = P × i × (1+i) n ÷ ((1+i) n − 1) P = loan amount · i = monthly rate (annual ÷ 12 ÷ 100) · n = number of monthly payments. Why your early payments are almost all interest Interest each month is charged on the outstanding balance , which is at its largest on day one. On a 250,000 loan at 5.5% over 20 years, the first payment is roughly 1,146 — of which about 1,146 × 55% is interest. By the final year almost the whole payment goes to principal. This is why the amortisation table above matters more than the headline rate: it shows where your money actually goes. Why overpaying is so effective An extra payment comes off the principal directly, so it removes not just that amount but every future month of interest that amount would have generated. On a long loan, a modest overpayment early can cut years off the term. Enter a figure in the extra-payment field to see the exact saving on your own numbers. What this does not include Processing fees, insurance, early-settlement penalties and rate changes on a variable loan are not modelled. Check whether your lender charges a prepayment penalty before overpaying — in some markets it cancels out the benefit.
#### Questions
Q: What does EMI stand for?
A: Equated Monthly Instalment — a fixed monthly payment covering both interest and principal, so the loan is fully repaid by the end of the term.
Q: Why is my total repayment so much more than the loan?
A: Because interest is charged every month on the balance still outstanding. On a 20-year loan at 5.5% you repay roughly 165% of what you borrowed. The amortisation table shows the split year by year.
Q: Does paying extra reduce my EMI or my term?
A: By default most lenders keep the EMI the same and shorten the term, which is what this calculator models. Some will instead recalculate a lower EMI over the original term. Ask your lender which they do — shortening the term saves far more interest.
Q: Is this the same as a mortgage calculator?
A: The payment maths is identical. A mortgage additionally involves a deposit, property price and affordability limits — use the mortgage affordability calculator for that.
Q: Does it handle variable or floating rates?
A: No. It assumes the rate is fixed for the whole term. For a floating loan, run it once at today's rate and again a few points higher to see your exposure.

### Mortgage Affordability Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/mortgage-affordability-calculator/
What you can realistically borrow — and whether you could still pay if rates rose.
#### How lenders decide what you can borrow
Market / product | Typical maximum DTI
Conservative / conforming | 36%
US qualified mortgage | 43%
Many GCC banks | 50% of salary (regulator-capped)
UK affordability model | Income multiple ~4.5× plus a stress test
Almost every lender in the world applies some version of the same three tests. The binding one is usually debt-to-income . 1. Debt-to-income (DTI) Your total monthly debt payments — the new mortgage plus car finance, credit cards and personal loans — must stay under a percentage of gross monthly income. Common limits: Enter the limit that applies to you. Using a lower figure than the maximum is how you leave yourself room. 2. Deposit / loan-to-value The deposit does not affect the monthly payment maths — it raises the price you can reach, one-for-one. It also drives the rate you are offered: most lenders price in tiers at 90%, 80% and 75% loan-to-value, and a larger deposit often removes mortgage insurance entirely. 3. The stress test — the part most calculators omit Regulators in the UK, EU, Canada and Australia require lenders to check you could still pay if rates rose by roughly two percentage points. This calculator runs that test for you. If the stressed maximum is far below the headline maximum, borrowing the full amount is a bet on rates staying low.
#### Questions
Q: Should I borrow the maximum I am offered?
A: Usually not. The maximum is the point at which a lender still expects to be repaid, not the point at which your life stays comfortable. The stress-test figure is a better guide to a safe borrowing level.
Q: Does a bigger deposit reduce my monthly payment?
A: It reduces the amount borrowed, so yes. It also commonly unlocks a lower rate band and can remove mortgage insurance, so the effect is larger than the headline number suggests.
Q: What counts as an existing debt payment?
A: Contractual monthly commitments: car finance, personal loans, student loans, credit-card minimums and any maintenance orders. Ordinary living costs like groceries and utilities are not counted in DTI, though lenders assess them separately.
Q: Why does the calculator ignore property taxes and insurance?
A: Because they vary enormously by country — some markets bundle them into the payment, others bill them annually and some have none at all. Deduct your local figure from the available-for-mortgage line for a stricter result.
Q: Is a 50% DTI safe just because a bank allows it?
A: A regulator-permitted ceiling is a limit on the lender, not a recommendation for you. At 50% DTI, half your gross income is committed before tax, housing costs and savings — most household budgets get very fragile there.

### Overtime Pay Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/overtime-pay-calculator/
Work out overtime from a salary or an hourly rate, at whichever multipliers your law or contract uses.
#### How overtime pay is calculated
Situation | Typical multiplier
US federal minimum for non-exempt staff (FLSA); a common contractual rate elsewhere. UK law sets no overtime premium. | 1.5× — "time and a half"
UAE daytime overtime | 1.25× of basic
UAE overtime between 22:00 and 04:00 | 1.5× of basic
Saudi Arabia overtime | 1.5× of wage
Rest day worked (many jurisdictions) | 1.5× plus a compensatory day
Public holidays / Sundays | 2× — "double time"
Overtime is your ordinary hourly rate multiplied by a premium. The two things that vary between countries are how the hourly rate is derived from a salary and which multiplier applies when . Deriving the hourly rate from a monthly salary hourly = (monthly salary × 12) ÷ (standard hours per week × 52) On a 6,000 monthly salary and a 48-hour week: (6,000 × 12) ÷ (48 × 52) = 28.85 an hour. Common multipliers worldwide These are the common defaults, not a substitute for your own contract or labour code — many collective agreements are more generous, and several countries base the premium on basic salary rather than gross. Basic versus gross This matters more than the multiplier. Several Gulf labour laws compute overtime on basic salary, excluding housing and transport allowances — so an employee on 6,000 gross with 3,600 basic has overtime calculated on 3,600. Enter whichever figure your law uses.
#### Questions
Q: What is time and a half?
A: Pay at 1.5 times the normal hourly rate. It is the most common overtime premium worldwide and the statutory US rate for hours beyond 40 in a week.
Q: Is overtime calculated on basic or gross salary?
A: It depends on the jurisdiction. Much of Europe and the US use total ordinary pay; several Gulf labour codes use basic salary only, excluding allowances. Using the wrong base is the single most common overtime error.
Q: How many hours before overtime starts?
A: Commonly 40 a week in the US and much of Europe, 48 across much of the Gulf and Asia. Some countries also trigger overtime on a daily threshold, typically 8 or 9 hours, regardless of the weekly total.
Q: Are managers entitled to overtime?
A: Often not. Most systems exempt genuine senior, supervisory or professional roles, but the test is the actual duties performed, not the job title. A title of 'manager' alone does not remove the entitlement.
Q: Can overtime be paid as time off instead?
A: In many countries yes, if the employee agrees — usually at the same premium, so 1.5 hours off for each overtime hour. Some jurisdictions require the employee's written consent.

### Percentage Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/percentage-calculator/
Six different percentage questions in one tool — with the formula shown, so you can check the working.
#### The six percentage formulas
Question | Formula | Example
What is A% of B? | A ÷ 100 × B | 25% of 200 = 50
A is what % of B? | A ÷ B × 100 | 50 of 200 = 25%
% change A → B | (B − A) ÷ |A| × 100 | 200 → 250 = +25%
Increase A by B% | A × (1 + B ÷ 100) | 200 + 25% = 250
Decrease A by B% | A × (1 − B ÷ 100) | 200 − 25% = 150
A is B% of what? | A ÷ (B ÷ 100) | 50 is 25% of 200
Why a decrease then an increase does not return you to the start Take 100, cut it by 20% to get 80, then add 20% back: 80 × 1.2 = 96, not 100. The second percentage is applied to a smaller base. To reverse a 20% decrease you need a 25% increase. This is the single most common percentage mistake, and it appears constantly in discount and salary-cut arithmetic. Percentage points versus percent If a rate moves from 5% to 7%, that is a rise of two percentage points but a 40% increase in the rate itself. Both statements are true and they describe the same change — mixing them up is a common source of misleading claims in reporting. Percent change when the starting value is negative The formula divides by the absolute value of A, so a move from −50 to −25 registers as a 50% improvement rather than a −50% one. Percent change on quantities that cross zero is ambiguous by nature and is usually better reported as an absolute difference.
#### Questions
Q: How do I calculate a percentage increase?
A: Subtract the old value from the new one, divide by the old value, then multiply by 100. From 200 to 250: (250 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 25%.
Q: Why doesn't reversing a percentage get me back to the original?
A: Because the second percentage applies to a different base. A 20% fall needs a 25% rise to undo it, since the rise is calculated on the reduced figure.
Q: What is the difference between percent and percentage points?
A: A move from 5% to 7% is two percentage points, but a 40% increase in the rate. Percentage points measure the gap between two percentages; percent measures relative change.
Q: How do I work out the original price before a discount?
A: Use the reverse mode. If an item costs 80 after a 20% discount, it was 80 ÷ 0.80 = 100 originally.
Q: Can percent change be more than 100%?
A: Yes for increases — doubling is +100%, tripling is +200%. Decreases cannot go below −100%, because that would mean the value fell past zero.

### Pro-Rata Salary Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/pro-rata-salary-calculator/
What a part-time or part-year role actually pays — the calculation employers get wrong most often.
#### How pro-rata pay is calculated
Method | How it works | Effect
Calendar-day | Annual ÷ 365 × days employed | Used here. Neutral across months.
Working-day | Monthly ÷ working days in that month × days worked | Slightly favours joiners in short months
Pro rata means "in proportion". Two proportions can apply at once, and the calculation multiplies both: pay = full-time salary × (your hours ÷ full-time hours) × (days worked ÷ 365) The two reductions are independent Someone working 24 hours against a 40-hour full-time week is on 60% FTE . If they also only work seven months of the year, they receive 60% of the salary for 7/12 of the year — about 35% of the full-time annual figure. Confusing these two reductions, or applying only one, is the most common payroll error in part-time contracts. Mid-month joiners and leavers Employers use one of two conventions and they give different answers: If your contract or local law specifies one, use that. The difference is usually small but it is real, and it is worth checking on a final settlement. What is normally pro-rated too Annual leave entitlement, bonuses and in many countries end-of-service benefits are all pro-rated on the same FTE basis. Part-time employees are generally entitled to the same proportion of benefits, not a reduced rate of pay per hour — paying a lower hourly rate purely for being part-time is unlawful discrimination in much of the world.
#### Questions
Q: What does pro rata actually mean on a job advert?
A: It means the advertised salary is the full-time figure and you will be paid the proportion matching your hours. A role advertised at 60,000 pro rata for 3 days a week actually pays about 36,000.
Q: How do I calculate pro-rata annual leave?
A: Multiply the full-time entitlement by your FTE percentage. At 60% FTE with a 25-day full-time allowance, you get 15 days. If you work fixed days, it is usually cleaner to count leave in hours.
Q: Should part-time staff get a lower hourly rate?
A: No. In most jurisdictions, paying a lower hourly rate solely because someone is part-time is unlawful. The total is lower because the hours are fewer, not because the rate is.
Q: Which is right for a mid-month start — calendar days or working days?
A: Both are used. Calendar-day is the more common default and the one applied here. Check your contract, since the two methods can differ by a few percent in a given month.
Q: Does pro rata affect end-of-service or gratuity?
A: Usually yes. Most systems base end-of-service on the actual salary paid and the length of service, so a part-time salary produces a proportionally smaller benefit. Country rules vary — see the country calculators.

### Retirement & FIRE Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/retirement-savings-calculator/
What you are on track for, what you actually need, and the age the gap closes.
#### How the projection works
Step 1 — grow what you have Your current savings and each monthly contribution are compounded at your expected return, month by month, until your target retirement age. Step 2 — work out what you will actually need This is the step most retirement calculators skip. The spending you enter is in today's money, so it is inflated forward to your retirement year, then converted into a required pot using the safe withdrawal rate: required pot = (annual spending × (1 + inflation) years ) ÷ withdrawal rate At 36,000 a year of spending and a 4% withdrawal rate, you need 900,000 in today's money — but 25 years of 3% inflation turns that into roughly 1.88 million of actual currency. Step 3 — find the crossover The financial independence age is the first year your projected pot exceeds the pot you would need in that year . Both numbers move, which is why the answer is rarely the age people assume. About the 4% rule The 4% safe withdrawal rate comes from the 1998 Trinity Study of historical US market data, which found a 4% initial withdrawal adjusted for inflation survived 30 years in almost all historical periods. It is a useful anchor, not a law. Reasons to use a lower figure: a retirement longer than 30 years, higher fees, a less diversified or non-US portfolio, or starting into a poor sequence of returns. Many practitioners now use 3.25–3.5% for early retirement. What is not modelled State or workplace pensions, end-of-service benefits, property, tax on withdrawals, and healthcare costs are all excluded. If you expect a state pension, subtract it from your target annual spending before entering the figure.
#### Questions
Q: How much do I need to retire?
A: A common starting point is 25 times your annual spending, which is the inverse of the 4% withdrawal rate. The critical adjustment is inflation: 25× your spending today is not 25× what that spending will cost when you actually retire.
Q: Is the 4% rule still safe?
A: It is a historical benchmark from US data over 30-year periods, not a guarantee. For a retirement of 40 years or more, or a portfolio with higher fees or less diversification, many planners use 3.25% to 3.5% instead.
Q: Should I include my house?
A: Generally no, unless you intend to sell it and live on the proceeds. A home you live in does not generate the income the withdrawal-rate method assumes.
Q: What return should I assume?
A: Be conservative. Long-run global equities have historically returned roughly 7% before inflation, but a portfolio holding bonds or cash will return less, and fees come off the top. Running the calculation at two different rates shows how sensitive your plan is.
Q: What if the calculator says I never reach independence?
A: It means contributions and returns never overtake inflated spending on these inputs. The three levers are contributing more, spending less in retirement, or working longer — and the first two are usually far more powerful than chasing a higher return.

### Salary Converter
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/salary-converter/
Convert any pay rate to any other — using your actual working pattern, not a generic 40-hour assumption.
#### How the conversion works
From | To annual
Hourly | rate × hours per week × paid weeks
Daily | rate × days per week × paid weeks
Weekly | rate × paid weeks
Monthly | rate × 12
Everything is converted through a single annual figure, then divided back out: Why "paid weeks per year" changes the answer This is the field generic converters get wrong. If you are salaried with paid annual leave, you are paid for all 52 weeks even though you work fewer — so use 52. If you are a contractor who is only paid for weeks actually worked, and you take four unpaid weeks off, use 48 . The same headline day rate produces a materially different annual figure depending on which applies to you. The 2,080-hour convention Many US-centric tools hard-code 2,080 hours (40 × 52). That is fine for a standard American full-time job and wrong nearly everywhere else — a 45-hour week is standard across much of the Gulf, 35 hours is common in France, and part-time patterns fit none of them. Setting your own hours and days is why the numbers here match your payslip. Gross, not net All figures are before income tax, social insurance and any employee contributions. Some countries also pay a statutory 13th month, which is not included here — add it to the annual figure if it applies to you.
#### Questions
Q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary?
A: Multiply the hourly rate by your hours per week, then by the number of paid weeks in the year. At 25 an hour, 40 hours a week and 52 paid weeks, that is 52,000 a year gross.
Q: Should I use 52 weeks or fewer?
A: Use 52 if you are salaried with paid holiday, because you are paid across the whole year. Use fewer only if there are weeks you genuinely are not paid for, which is typical for contractors and some hourly roles.
Q: Is this gross or net pay?
A: Gross — before income tax, social security and any deductions. Net pay depends entirely on your country's tax rules and personal circumstances.
Q: How do I handle a 13th-month salary or annual bonus?
A: Add it to the annual total separately. A guaranteed 13th month effectively multiplies a monthly salary by 13 rather than 12.
Q: Why does my monthly figure differ slightly from four weekly payments?
A: Because a month averages about 4.33 weeks, not 4. Four weekly payments is roughly 92% of a true month, which is why weekly-paid workers get five payments in some months.

### VAT & GST Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/vat-gst-calculator/
Add tax to a net price, or extract the tax already inside a gross price.
#### How VAT and GST are calculated
Type | How it works | Where
VAT | Charged at each stage; businesses reclaim input tax so only the end consumer bears it | EU, UK, GCC, most of Africa and Latin America
GST | Mechanically the same as VAT, different name; India splits it into CGST/SGST/IGST | India, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Singapore
Sales tax | Charged only at final sale, no input reclaim; rates stack by state and city | United States
Adding tax to a net price tax = net × rate ÷ 100 1,000 net at 5% → 50 tax → 1,050 gross. Removing tax from a gross price — the one people get wrong You cannot simply take the percentage off a gross figure. To strip 5% tax out of 1,050, subtracting 5% gives 997.50, which is wrong. The correct formula divides: net = gross ÷ (1 + rate ÷ 100) 1,050 ÷ 1.05 = 1,000 net, so the tax is 50. The error grows with the rate: at 20% the naive method understates the net price by 4%. VAT, GST and sales tax are not quite the same thing US sales tax is not included in the preset list because there is no national rate — the combined state and local rate varies by address, from zero in several states to over 10% in parts of Louisiana and Tennessee. Reduced and zero rates The presets are standard rates. Most countries apply reduced rates to food, medicine, books, children's clothing and transport, and zero-rate exports. India's GST runs in slabs of 0, 5, 12, 18 and 28%. Always confirm which rate applies to the specific goods or service.
#### Questions
Q: How do I remove VAT from a total?
A: Divide the gross amount by 1 plus the rate as a decimal. To remove 20% VAT, divide by 1.20. Do not subtract 20% from the gross figure — that gives the wrong answer.
Q: What is the difference between VAT and GST?
A: Very little in mechanism. Both are value-added taxes collected in stages with input-tax recovery for businesses. The name differs by country, and India's GST is split into central and state components.
Q: Why is US sales tax not in the list?
A: Because the US has no national rate. Sales tax is set by states, counties and cities, so the combined rate depends on the delivery address. Five states levy no state sales tax at all.
Q: Which rate applies to my product?
A: The standard rate unless your product is in a reduced, zero-rated or exempt category — commonly food, medicine, books, education and healthcare. Check your tax authority's schedule; the categories are specific and often counter-intuitive.
Q: Is the tax on the discounted price or the original?
A: On the price actually charged, after discount. If you discount 1,000 to 900, tax is calculated on 900.

### Working Days Calculator
URL: https://calcnate.com/tools/working-days-calculator/
Business days between two dates — with the weekend your country actually uses, not just Saturday–Sunday.
#### How working days are counted
Pattern | Where
Saturday & Sunday | Europe, the Americas, most of Asia, and the UAE public sector since 2022 (which moved to a half-day Friday)
Friday & Saturday | Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, and many UAE private-sector employers
Friday only | Some single-day-weekend employers across South Asia and the Middle East
Thursday & Friday | The historic Gulf pattern, still found in some legacy contracts
The calculator steps through every date from start to end inclusive, classifies each by its day of the week, and subtracts the days that fall on your chosen weekend — then subtracts any public holidays you enter. Why a configurable weekend matters Most online business-day calculators hard-code Saturday and Sunday, which quietly produces wrong answers for a large part of the world. Weekend patterns actually in use include: Pick the pattern in your own contract. If your employer runs a half-day Friday, count it as a working day and adjust the hours separately. Inclusive counting Both endpoints are included, so 1 March to 31 March returns 31 calendar days. This matches how notice periods, probation and leave are normally counted in employment contracts. If you need the gap between two dates rather than the span, subtract one. Public holidays Holiday dates differ by country and several — including Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha — move each year with the lunar calendar, so they are entered as a number rather than guessed. Count only the holidays that fall on days you would otherwise have worked; a holiday landing on your weekend does not add a day off.
#### Questions
Q: Does the calculator include both the start and end date?
A: Yes. A range from 1 March to 31 March counts as 31 calendar days. This matches standard employment-contract practice for notice and leave periods.
Q: Which weekend should I choose for the UAE?
A: It depends on the employer. The UAE public sector moved to Saturday–Sunday with a half-day Friday in January 2022, but many private-sector companies kept Friday–Saturday. Check your own contract.
Q: Why enter holidays as a number instead of picking a country?
A: Because public holidays vary by emirate, state and province, and Islamic holidays shift each year with moon sighting — often confirmed only days in advance. A number you control is more accurate than a stale built-in list.
Q: Can I use this for a notice period?
A: Yes, but check what your contract counts. Most notice periods run in calendar days, not working days, so the total-calendar-days figure is usually the relevant one.
Q: How many working days are in a year?
A: About 260 on a five-day week before public holidays — 365 days minus 104 weekend days. Subtract your local holidays, typically 8 to 15, for the real figure.
